headline: Cool Nights, Green Water — Albies Show Early on the Southwest Ledge
subhead: The first cold snap of September flipped a switch on Block Island, and the rips are answering with albies, bonito, and bass starting to stack on bunker.
body_markdown:
You feel it before you see it out here. The air changed sometime around the full moon this weekend — that first real snap of September, where the humidity drops out and the nights get that clean, cold edge to them. Stand on the bluffs at Mohegan or look out past the breakwater at New Harbor and the water's got a different color to it now, a deeper green pushing into the blue instead of the milky summer haze. That's the tell. Block Island runs on its own clock, and this week it told the fleet fall is coming whether the calendar agrees or not.

The biggest story right now is the albies. They showed up early and they showed up hot, working bait on the Southwest Ledge and pushing bonito out ahead of them into the same rips. We flagged this pattern last week — said the false albacore would follow the bonito in behind them within a week to ten days, with the Ledge and the North Rip the spots to check daily — and that's exactly how it's playing out. Boats working the Ledge on the last two hours of the ebb are finding albies busting on peanut bunker and rain bait, green-and-white or pink-and-white epoxy jigs doing the work, worked fast on light spin gear. Bonito are mixed right in with them, same structure, same speed retrieve, though the albies have been the more consistent player through the week.

Striped bass are the other half of the equation, and they're moving into their early-fall staging pattern right on schedule. Bunker schools are tightening up around the island — you can see it from a distance now, bait balled tight and nervous instead of scattered thin like it was in August. That's a direct result of the building moon and the cooling nights pulling bait and predators into the same real estate. The North Rip has been holding fish on the pushing tide, working the deeper edge where the rip stands up hardest against the current — that's where the 40-pound class bass like to sit, tucked down in the color change waiting for something to get pushed off balance. Live bunker on a fish-finder rig, or a bunker chunk fished on the bottom just off the edge of the rip, has been the play for anyone willing to sit on it through a tide change. Trolling bunker spoons or umbrella rigs along the edge of the Ledge on the last of the outgoing has also produced, though the fish have been more willing to show themselves on the harder push of water than on slack.

The new moon coming September 10 is the number to circle. Every year it works the same way out here — the tide gets more aggressive, the bait gets pushed harder against structure, and that's usually the trigger for the first real blitz behavior of the fall. Right now the bass are still in that staging mode, picking at bait rather than committing to it, but that's about to change. If the pattern holds the way it usually does, expect the North Rip and the Southwest Ledge to go from a good pick to genuine blitz water sometime in the ten days after the new moon, especially on the dawn and dusk pushes when the light is low and the bass feel bold enough to come up.

Bluefish have stayed steady through all of this, and they're not subtle about it. Choppers in the 4 to 8-pound range are working the same bunker schools as the bass, and they'll hit anything moving fast — bucktails, diamond jigs, poppers worked hard on the surface early and late. If you're marking bait on the sounder anywhere between the Ledge and the North Rip, there's a good chance blues are under it even when the bass aren't showing.

Fluke are winding down, which is normal for this point in September. There's still a fishable pick in the deeper water off Great Salt Pond and along the drop toward the Ledge, working Gulp on bucktails tipped with squid strips, but the bite has lost the consistency it had in July and August. Most of the fleet has already shifted attention toward the bass and albies, and that's the right move — the fluke window here is closing fast as the fish start their move offshore.

Porgies and blackfish are still around structure inshore, but with everything else happening on the surface right now, nobody's spending much time on them, and that's fine — there'll be time for tautog later in the fall when the water cools further and the bass move on.

Looking ahead, the next several days should keep building. If the wind stays reasonable out of the northwest — which tends to clean the water and stack bait against the rips rather than scatter it — the albie and bonito bite on the Southwest Ledge should hold steady or improve, and the bass at the North Rip should keep tightening up as bait gets pushed harder by the approaching new moon tide. Best case, that new moon push on the 10th kicks off the first real blitz of the fall, with bass, blues, and albies all working the same stretch of water at once. If it slides a few days either way, the pattern doesn't change — it just shifts the calendar. Either way, this is the window locals wait all summer for. The water's cooling, the bait's tightening, and the Ledge is already showing what's coming.
